ch91.essay:
This is the funniest chapter in the book, and I think it's funny in a very specific way: it's a comedy of translation. Stubb says one thing, the Guernsey mate says another, and the French captain — a cologne manufacturer on his first voyage, which is its own perfect joke on a ship called the Rose-bud that stinks — hears a third. Melville lets us hold all three at once, and the pleasure is watching the gap widen. "Tell him he's a baboon" becomes "he conjures us, as we value our lives, to cut loose from these fish." Nobody is lying to anyone who could understand them.

What I keep noticing is how carefully the chapter is engineered as a *nose* chapter. The Pequod finds the ship by smell before sight; the sailors' noses project "like so many jib-booms"; the mate has his nose in a bag; Stubb claims a wax nose. And then the ambergris — the whole point — arrives as a single thread of perfume flowing through the stench "as one river will flow into and then along with another, without at all blending." That image is doing real work: it's the book's habit of finding the precious thing inside the rotten thing, done as physical fact rather than sermon.

And there's a shadow on it. Stubb's aside — "I've diddled him, and (aside to himself) perhaps somebody else" — is a confession that he's also cheating Ahab, who cares nothing for ambergris and hauls him back mid-dig. The one man on board who treats the voyage as ordinary commerce has to steal his profit under the captain's nose. It's a light chapter, but it's also the last really light one.

annotations.quote: the many noses on the Pequod’s deck proved more vigilant discoverers than the three pairs of eyes aloft
annotations.note: Melville opens by demoting sight. A whole book has been organized around lookouts and mast-heads, and here the crew finds its prize by stink. Notice how many noses show up in the next few pages — it becomes the chapter's running organ.

annotations.quote: worse than an Assyrian city in the plague, when the living are incompetent to bury the departed
annotations.note: A rotting whale compared to a plague city. Melville's comparisons keep leaping in scale — a carcass becomes a civilization — and that habit is one of the book's signatures: nothing stays its own size for long.

annotations.quote: he was a Cologne manufacturer before
annotations.note: The captain of the Rose-bud, a ship that reeks, is a perfume-maker on his first voyage. Melville rarely explains his jokes; this one he trusts you to assemble yourself, and it lands harder for it.

annotations.quote: “Oh, nothing! It’s a wax nose; I have to hold it on.
annotations.note: Stubb's deadpan is his whole character in one line. He's holding his nose against the stench, is caught, and invents a prosthetic on the spot — a comic echo, I think, of the ivory limbs that are about to dominate the next several chapters.

annotations.quote: “Why,” said Stubb, eyeing the velvet vest and the watch and seals, “you may as well begin by telling him that he looks a sort of babyish to me, though I don’t pretend to be a judge.”
annotations.note: Here begins the three-way translation game. Read the next dozen exchanges as a triptych: what Stubb says, what the mate says he said, and what the captain does. The comedy lives in the widening gap, and everyone is sincere.

annotations.quote: tell him I’ve diddled him, and (aside to himself) perhaps somebody else.”
annotations.note: The 'somebody else' is Ahab. Stubb is confessing, in an aside, that his ambergris scheme is a theft from a captain who would never permit the delay — and when Ahab yanks him back mid-dig, that's exactly what happens.

annotations.quote: there stole a faint stream of perfume, which flowed through the tide of bad smells without being absorbed by it, as one river will flow into and then along with another, without at all blending with it for a time
annotations.note: This is my favorite sentence in the chapter. The hydrological image — two rivers running side by side unmixed — is precise and quietly beautiful, and it's the physical form of a spiritual idea Melville states outright in the next chapter: incorruption found in the heart of decay.

annotations.quote: something that looked like ripe Windsor soap, or rich mottled old cheese; very unctuous and savory withal
annotations.note: Notice how Ishmael describes treasure: soap, cheese, something you could dent with a thumb. Melville nearly always domesticates the sublime with kitchen and bathroom imagery, and the effect isn't deflation — it's that the ordinary gets promoted.

links.why: The ambergris Stubb swindles out of the Rose-bud is explained — and made beautiful — in the very next chapter.
The other comic gam with a foreign ship, the German Virgin; Melville's comedy of nations in two installments.
What a gam is supposed to be, before Stubb turns one into a con.

ch92.essay:
A two-page chapter that manages to touch commerce, Parliament, cooking, Corinthians, and anti-Semitism in the Middle Ages. That's the Melville digression at its most compressed — and I find it more interesting than it first looks, because the structure is a swerve. Ishmael sets up a genuinely lovely thought ("is this nothing?") — incorruptible fragrance found inside a diseased, decaying animal, sown in dishonor and raised in glory — and then, exactly when he'd like to end, he says he *cannot*, because he has to rebut a slander against whalemen. The high thought is abandoned for a defensive PR campaign about whether whales smell.

I think that's deliberate and funny, and also honest about how minds actually work: you have your transcendent moment and then you remember the thing you're annoyed about. But the sermon that got cut short is still the real center. Ambergris is the book's clearest emblem of something it keeps insisting on — that beauty, value, and meaning turn up in the wrong places, in bowels and blubber-rooms and among cannibals, and that the dainty ladies who wear the perfume would be sick to know where it came from. The whole novel is a version of that claim about its own subject.

The Cologne-water line is the tell: the sweetest thing is the worst-smelling in its making. Melville wrote this book in a state of what he called 'the greatest calm' amid financial and family pressure, and I can't help reading the passage as partly about writing.

annotations.quote: Who would think, then, that such fine ladies and gentlemen should regale themselves with an essence found in the inglorious bowels of a sick whale!
annotations.note: The whole chapter — maybe the whole book — in one exclamation. Melville loves the gap between the polished thing and its grubby origin, and he'll play it again with the try-works, the lamp, and the pulpit-shaped mincing horse.

annotations.quote: Now that the incorruption of this most fragrant ambergris should be found in the heart of such decay; is this nothing?
annotations.note: 'Is this nothing?' is a question Ishmael keeps asking the reader in different forms. Here he answers it with St. Paul — sown in dishonor, raised in glory — and then, to my delight, interrupts his own homily to argue about smells.

annotations.quote: I should like to conclude the chapter with the above appeal, but cannot, owing to my anxiety to repel a charge often made against whalemen
annotations.note: A narrator admitting he'd prefer to stop on the high note but is too irritated to. This is one of the most human moments in the book: the transcendent thought loses out to a grievance.

annotations.quote: Cologne-water, in its rudimental manufacturing stages, is the worst.
annotations.note: Sweetest product, foulest process. Keep this line in mind for The Try-Works four chapters on — and, if you like, for the book itself, a foul-smelling manufacture that came out as perfume.

annotations.quote: the motion of a Sperm Whale’s flukes above water dispenses a perfume, as when a musk-scented lady rustles her dress in a warm parlor
annotations.note: Melville pushes his rebuttal one step past plausible and into gallantry — a ninety-ton whale as a lady in a parlor. I'm never sure whether he's joking here; I think the not-being-sure is the point.

links.why: Where this ambergris came from — a rotting whale a Frenchman was glad to be rid of.

links.q: Such a clearer! such a sweetener!
links.why: Two chapters on, the other fragrant thing the whale yields, and what it does to Ishmael.
The whale's other paradox of surface and interior — thin skin, thick blanket.

ch93.essay:
I find this the hardest chapter in the book to read, and the one I would defend hardest, so let me try to say exactly why it works rather than just that it does. It opens with a chiasmus — 'a most significant event befell the most insignificant of the Pequod's crew' — and that sentence is a promise about structure. Melville is telling you the book's hierarchy of importance is about to invert, and that Pip, the ship-keeper nobody wanted in a boat, will become 'a living and ever accompanying prophecy' of the ship's end. Everything that follows is the mechanism by which a comic minor character is converted into an oracle, and the mechanism has three parts: a rope, a price, and a calm.

The rope first. In [[ch60:enveloped in whale-lines|The Line]] Ishmael told us that 'all men live enveloped in whale-lines,' and that the difference between a sailor and a landsman is only that the sailor knows it. Here the line takes 'several turns around his chest and neck' and drags a boy foaming to the chocks. The abstraction of Chapter 60 becomes a blue, choked face that 'plainly looked, Do, for God's sake!' — a face that speaks a sentence. Then the price. Stubb, the book's most likable officer, the man who goes to everything laughing, is the one who says 'a whale would sell for thirty times what you would, Pip, in Alabama.' Pip is a free Black boy from Tolland County, Connecticut; Stubb, meaning to be practical, appraises him as a slave. Ishmael's gloss — 'man is a money-making animal, which propensity too often interferes with his benevolence' — is so understated it is almost a joke, and I think the understatement is the point. Melville does not editorialize; he lets you hear a decent man price a child, and lets the sentence sit.

Then the calm, which is the part that undoes me. The second abandonment happens on 'a beautiful, bounteous, blue day,' the sea 'like gold-beater's skin hammered out to the extremest,' Pip's head 'like a head of cloves.' Melville's cruelest scenes are his loveliest — compare the way the whale glides in on the first day of the chase with 'a gentle joyousness' in [[ch133:A gentle joyousness|The Chase, First Day]]. The indifference of the universe is not a storm; it is a gorgeous calm that doesn't notice you. And the horror is named precisely: not drowning but 'the intense concentration of self in the middle of such a heartless immensity.' Read that beside Ahab. Ahab's whole condition is a self concentrated in a heartless immensity — but Ahab chose it, on the quarter-deck, and calls it purpose. Pip has it done to him, and calls it nothing, because it costs him speech.

The great paragraph is the one where the sea 'jeeringly kept his finite body up, but drowned the infinite of his soul.' Notice what Melville refuses to do: he refuses to say Pip was destroyed. The soul is 'not drowned entirely,' but 'carried down alive to wondrous depths,' where 'the miser-merman, Wisdom, revealed his hoarded heaps.' And what Pip sees is 'God's foot upon the treadle of the loom.' That loom is the one Ishmael wove in [[ch47:weaving away at the Fates|The Mat-Maker]] — chance, free will, and necessity — and it will return, deafening, in [[ch102:whither flows the fabric|A Bower in the Arsacides]]. Pip is the only character who sees the weaver directly. 'And spoke it; and therefore his shipmates called him mad.' The punishment is not for seeing but for saying. I take that as a warning Ishmael is issuing to himself: this whole narration is Pip's offense, committed at length.

Two last things. 'So man's insanity is heaven's sense' — I have never been able to decide whether this is the most consoling or the most despairing sentence in the book, and I now think the indecision is correct, because Melville built it to be both. Pip has been initiated; Pip has been ruined; the sentence declines to choose. And the final line: 'it will then be seen what like abandonment befell myself.' That is a direct promise of the [[epilogue|Epilogue]]. There are two castaways in this book. One is picked up by the ship and goes mad; one is picked up by the [[ch128:weeping for her children|Rachel]] and writes it all down. The chapter is a dress rehearsal, and when Ahab later tells Pip 'thou art tied to me by cords woven of my heart-strings' in [[ch125:cords woven of my heart-strings|The Log and Line]], you should hear the whale-line in the word cords.

annotations.quote: a most significant event befell the most insignificant of the Pequod’s crew
annotations.note: The chiasmus is the thesis. Melville is telling you, on the first line, that the book's hierarchy of importance is about to be inverted — and Pip, the ship-keeper nobody wanted in a boat, will become its prophet.

annotations.quote: For blacks, the year’s calendar should show naught but three hundred and sixty-five Fourth of Julys and New Year’s Days.
annotations.note: This paragraph is uncomfortable — affectionate, condescending, and racialized in the mode of 1851 — and I don't think you should read past it quickly. What's strange is where it goes: within a few lines Melville is insisting that 'even blackness has its brilliancy,' and building a diamond-in-the-dark image that becomes Pip's fate.

annotations.quote: the evil-blazing diamond, once the divinest symbol of the crystal skies, looks like some crown-jewel stolen from the King of Hell
annotations.note: A jeweler shows a diamond against black cloth under gaslight to make it blaze. Melville is telling you, before it happens, what madness will do to Pip: light him up unnaturally, and make his brilliance terrible.

annotations.quote: Meantime Pip’s blue, choked face plainly looked, Do, for God’s sake!
annotations.note: A face 'looking' a sentence. The line is throttling the boy, Tashtego's knife hangs over it, and the whole thing takes half a minute. Melville wants you to feel how fast a life is weighed.

annotations.quote: a whale would sell for thirty times what you would, Pip, in Alabama
annotations.note: The most brutal sentence in the book, and Stubb says it as advice. Pip is a free Black boy from Connecticut; Stubb, meaning to be practical, prices him as a slave — and 'in Alabama' is doing the work, because that is the only place the comparison makes sense. Melville's gloss, 'man is a money-making animal,' is bitterly understated, and I think the understatement is deliberate: he wants you to notice that nobody in the boat finds the sentence strange. The whole economy of the ship — the [[ch16:seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay|lays]], the doubloon, the oil — is compressed into one appraisal.

annotations.quote: It was a beautiful, bounteous, blue day; the spangled sea calm and cool
annotations.note: Notice that the abandonment happens in perfect weather. Melville's cruelest scenes are his loveliest — the indifference of the sea is not a storm, it's a gorgeous calm that doesn't notice you.

annotations.quote: The intense concentration of self in the middle of such a heartless immensity, my God! who can tell it?
annotations.note: Not the water but the *self* is the horror — a mind with nothing around it to answer back. This is why the chapter matters to the whole book: Ahab lives in exactly this condition, chosen on purpose and renamed as will. Melville even gives you the control: sailors bathing in a dead calm 'hug their ship' and coast along her sides, because the open sea is intolerable not to the body but to the mind.

annotations.quote: The sea had jeeringly kept his finite body up, but drowned the infinite of his soul.
annotations.note: Read it twice. The body floats and the soul sinks; the sea is 'jeering'; and yet what the soul finds at the bottom is not nothing but *wisdom*, 'the miser-merman' with his hoards. The sentence refuses to decide whether Pip was destroyed or initiated.

annotations.quote: He saw God’s foot upon the treadle of the loom, and spoke it; and therefore his shipmates called him mad.
annotations.note: The loom returns from [[ch47:weaving away at the Fates|The Mat-Maker]] and will return again in [[ch102:whither flows the fabric|the Arsacides]]. Here it's explicit: Pip sees the weaver at work. Note the exact grammar of the punishment — he saw it 'and spoke it; and *therefore* his shipmates called him mad.' The madness is a social verdict on the speaking, not a fact about the seeing. That is a hint about what Ishmael's own narration is risking, and about why he keeps hedging his own visions with jokes.

annotations.quote: in the sequel of the narrative, it will then be seen what like abandonment befell myself.
annotations.note: A straight promise of the Epilogue. Pip and Ishmael are the two castaways of the book — one goes mad and is picked up by the ship, one survives and is picked up by the Rachel. The chapter is a dress rehearsal.

annotations.quote: Stubb’s inexorable back was turned upon him; and the whale was winged.
annotations.note: Two short clauses, and the second is almost cheerful — 'winged' is a sporting word. Melville lets the hunt's vocabulary run straight over the abandoned boy without pausing, which is exactly how Stubb experiences it.

annotations.quote: another lonely castaway, though the loftiest and the brightest
annotations.note: 'Another' — the first lonely castaway is the sun itself, at the center of the sea. Melville makes Pip the sun's double for one sentence, and the word will be the title of the book's last page.

links.why: The line around Pip's neck is the one Ishmael abstracted here; read the two together and the abstraction gets a face.
The loom Pip sees God's foot upon is the one Ishmael and Queequeg were weaving on this quiet afternoon.
Pip's glimpse of the weaver becomes a full cosmology here — and the weaver turns out to be deaf.
Where Ahab takes the castaway in, and what he says about the cords between them.
The 'abandonment' promised in the last line; the second castaway is the one telling you the story.

ch94.essay:
Coming directly after [[ch93|The Castaway]], this chapter feels like a hand held out, and I want to be precise about what kind of hand. It is also, let's be honest, extremely funny and extremely bodily — a shipful of men sitting cross-legged around a 'Constantine's bath' of spermaceti, squeezing lumps back into fluid, squeezing each other's fingers by mistake, and looking into each other's eyes 'sentimentally.' Readers have argued since the 1920s about how homoerotic it is. I think the answer is obviously yes and also obviously something else, and the two are not in competition; what interests me is how Melville built a sentence that makes you unable to pick one.

Look at the shape of the big paragraph. It is a single sentence sustained by semicolons — 'as I sat there...; after the bitter exertion...; under a blue tranquil sky; the ship under indolent sail...; as I bathed my hands...; as they richly broke to my fingers...; as I snuffed up that uncontaminated aroma' — and only then does the main verb arrive: 'I declare to you.' The syntax is a bath. You are held in the subordinate clauses before you are let out. And what is declared is the one thing that matters for the plot: 'I forgot all about our horrible oath.' The oath is Ahab's, sworn on the [[ch36:Death to Moby Dick|quarter-deck]], and this is the only place in the book where Ishmael says he was freed from it. The freeing agent is not an argument — Ishmael has plenty of those and none of them work — but a physical sensation, warmth, and the smell of violets.

The joke that makes it a great chapter rather than a lovely one is that the universal love is an *accident of the work*. He is 'unwittingly squeezing my co-laborers' hands in it, mistaking their hands for the gentle globules.' The tenderness is not decided; it is a mistake produced by shared labor, and I find that far more moving than a resolution would be. Then the phrase 'the very milk and sperm of kindness' — Lady Macbeth's 'milk of human kindness,' spoken by her with contempt, rewritten with 'sperm' in it and turned from a sneer into a benediction. Erotic, comic, sacramental: Melville has arranged the words so that any one reading leaves out too much.

The sentence I would single out, and the one I think a first-time reader most easily slides past, is the one about lowering 'his conceit of attainable felicity; not placing it anywhere in the intellect or the fancy; but in the wife, the heart, the bed, the table, the saddle, the fireside, the country.' That list is the quiet counter-philosophy to Ahab, stated once and never again. Ahab has placed his felicity entirely in the intellect — in *solving*, in striking through the mask — and here, elbow-deep in whale fat, Ishmael says that the intellect is precisely the wrong place to put it. This is the same Ishmael who in [[ch1:the image of the ungraspable phantom of life|Loomings]] told you that the ungraspable phantom of life is 'the key to it all.' The Squeeze is where he lets the key go. And then the angels, 'each with his hands in a jar of spermaceti': I laugh every time, and it is also a real picture of heaven, because if felicity lives in the hands, then so does paradise.

The back half — white-horse, plum-pudding, slobgollion, gurry, nippers — is Melville doing what he always does after an ecstasy, which is go straight back to the inventory. It's worth noticing that the inventory is itself gorgeous: plum-pudding is 'plums of rubies, in pictures of citron,' gore described by a jeweler, and this is the same eye that will find beauty in the [[ch96|Try-Works]] fire. And the chapter ends in the blubber-room, at night, with a barefoot man standing on a sliding sheet of fat swinging a spade 'sharp as hone can make it,' and the flat line 'Toes are scarce among veteran blubber-room men.' Squeeze of the hand, loss of the toe. The book will not let you keep the meadow, and I have come to think that refusal is the tenderness — it does not lie to you about where the warmth was found.

annotations.quote: A sweet and unctuous duty!
annotations.note: After the Castaway, the tone snaps like a released spring. Watch how quickly the exclamation points arrive — 'Such a clearer! such a sweetener!' — Ishmael is almost giddy, and I think the giddiness is relief.

annotations.quote: I forgot all about our horrible oath; in that inexpressible sperm, I washed my hands and my heart of it
annotations.note: The oath is Ahab's — the vow sworn with the crossed lances on the [[ch36:Death to Moby Dick|quarter-deck]] to hunt the White Whale to the death. This is the only place Ishmael says he was freed from it, and notice the freeing agent: not an argument, which Ishmael has in abundance, but a temperature and a smell. The book's answer to monomania, when it finally comes, is tactile.

annotations.quote: I found myself unwittingly squeezing my co-laborers’ hands in it, mistaking their hands for the gentle globules
annotations.note: The comedy of this line is precise: he mistakes his shipmates for whale fat and *that* is what produces the universal love. The tenderness is an accident of the work. I find that more moving than a decision would be.

annotations.quote: let us all squeeze ourselves into each other; let us squeeze ourselves universally into the very milk and sperm of kindness.
annotations.note: 'Milk of human kindness' is Lady Macbeth's phrase, said with contempt; Melville rewrites it with 'sperm' in it, and turns a sneer into a benediction. Whether you find it erotic, comic, or sacramental, notice that he has made you unable to pick just one.

annotations.quote: man must eventually lower, or at least shift, his conceit of attainable felicity; not placing it anywhere in the intellect or the fancy; but in the wife, the heart, the bed, the table, the saddle, the fireside, the country
annotations.note: This is the quiet counter-philosophy to Ahab, stated once and never again. Happiness is not in solving; it's in small warm things — and read the list slowly, because it is arranged from the most intimate outward: wife, heart, bed, table, saddle, fireside, country. Ahab has placed his felicity in the intellect alone, which is the one place the sentence forbids. Ishmael says it, and then, being Ishmael, goes back to sea anyway — which is either a contradiction or the honest admission that knowing where felicity lives is not the same as being able to stay there.

annotations.quote: I saw long rows of angels in paradise, each with his hands in a jar of spermaceti.
annotations.note: The most cheerfully ridiculous image of heaven in American literature, and I don't think Melville is only joking. If felicity is in the hands, then so is paradise.

annotations.quote: It is plums of rubies, in pictures of citron.
annotations.note: Plum-pudding is a slab of whale flesh, and Melville describes it like a jeweler and a painter at once. He is teaching you to look at gore as color — a habit he'll ask you to keep through the Try-Works.

annotations.quote: It is called slobgollion; an appellation original with the whalemen, and even so is the nature of the substance.
annotations.note: Melville visibly enjoys the word. The little catalogue that follows — slobgollion, gurry, nippers — is a lexicographer's pleasure, and also a reminder that every trade builds a private language nobody ashore will ever learn.

annotations.quote: Toes are scarce among veteran blubber-room men.
annotations.note: The chapter that began in a meadow ends in a dark room with a barefoot man on a sliding sheet of fat and a razor-sharp spade. The book never lets a squeeze of the hand stand without a lost toe beside it.

annotations.quote: I declare to you, that for the time I lived as in a musky meadow
annotations.note: The main verb of a sentence that has been running for seven clauses. Melville makes you wait in the subordinate 'as... as... as...' the way the men sit in the bath; the grammar itself is the immersion, and 'I declare to you' arrives like a man surfacing.

links.why: Read the two as a pair: the loneliest page in the book, then the warmest, back to back — and the warmth is made of the same whale.
The 'horrible oath' Ishmael forgets here was sworn on this deck; you should feel how far the spermaceti has carried him from it.

links.q: Look not too long in the face of the fire
links.why: The same substance, two chapters on, becomes fire and smoke; Melville gives you the sacrament and then the furnace.

links.q: the image of the ungraspable phantom of life
links.why: Loomings puts the key to everything in the ungraspable; the Squeeze puts it in the wife, the bed, the table. Decide which Ishmael you believe.

ch95.essay:
Three paragraphs, and one of the boldest jokes in nineteenth-century fiction: the mincer wears the whale's penis as a cassock and stands at his 'pulpit' cutting 'bible leaves.' Melville never names the organ — 'that unaccountable cone,' the 'grandissimus' — and the reticence is part of the fun, a wink he assumes the reader will catch without help. What I like is that it isn't merely a dirty joke. He hangs it on a real biblical episode, Queen Maachah's idol burnt at the brook Kedron, so the thing on the deck is an idol, the man is a priest, and the whole operation — mincing blubber thin so the oil comes out better — is a liturgy.

The sacrilege is the point. Melville's religious feeling in this book is intense and unstable: he'll give you Father Mapple's sermon and then this, and I don't think he considered them opposites. Both are about what men do with something enormous they can't understand — dress it, name it, cut it into leaves. 'What a candidate for an archbishopric, what a lad for a Pope were this mincer!' has an edge of contempt for actual popes, and an edge of respect for actual mincers.

Also: this is the chapter that most reliably made 1851 reviewers uncomfortable, and I suspect Melville knew it would and kept it short so it couldn't be excerpted without being obvious.

annotations.quote: that unaccountable cone,—longer than a Kentuckian is tall, nigh a foot in diameter at the base, and jet-black as Yojo
annotations.note: Melville never says the word. He measures it against a Kentuckian and compares it to Queequeg's idol, and trusts you to work it out. The refusal to name is the joke's engine — and the comparison to Yojo quietly makes it a god.

annotations.quote: for worshipping which, King Asa, her son, did depose her, and destroyed the idol, and burnt it for an abomination at the brook Kedron
annotations.note: He grounds the phallic idol in 1 Kings 15. Whether or not Maachah's idol really was such a thing (scholars have argued), Melville wants the scene to carry real scriptural weight so that the sacrilege has something to push against.

annotations.quote: The mincer now stands before you invested in the full canonicals of his calling.
annotations.note: 'Canonicals' is a clergyman's robe. The sentence is straight-faced, which is why it's funny; and the image — a man dressed in the whale's skin, pulling it on 'like a pantaloon leg' — is also a small prophecy of how the whale ends up wearing men.

annotations.quote: Arrayed in decent black; occupying a conspicuous pulpit; intent on bible leaves; what a candidate for an archbishopric, what a lad for a Pope were this mincer!*
annotations.note: Three ecclesiastical terms in a row and an asterisk to explain that 'bible leaves' is genuine whaler slang for thin slices. Melville is delighted that the real vocabulary of the trade handed him the blasphemy ready-made.

links.why: The sacrament of the sperm is immediately followed by this obscene-priestly joke; Melville never lets the tone settle.
The mincer's 'bible leaves' feed the try-pots in the next chapter.

ch96.essay:
If I had to choose one chapter to show what this book can do, it might be this one, because it does three completely different things in eleven paragraphs and each one turns on the last. It begins as engineering: brick kilns bolted to a wooden deck, try-pots polished 'like silver punch-bowls,' cynical old sailors curled up asleep in them, and Ishmael, scrubbing one with a soapstone, discovering that all bodies sliding down a cycloid reach the bottom in the same time. That is a real theorem — Huygens's tautochrone, 1659 — and it's the book's method in miniature: the highest abstraction found inside the lowliest labor. You are meant to remember this tone, because the chapter is about to abandon it.

Then Stubb says 'fire the works,' and the prose catches. The whale 'burns by his own body' — 'like a plethoric burning martyr, or a self-consuming misanthrope,' and it is hard not to hear Ahab in 'self-consuming.' The smoke 'smells like the left wing of the day of judgment; it is an argument for the pit' — two jokes stacked, since Judgment Day has a *left wing* (the damned side of every altarpiece) and the stench out-argues any theologian. And then the paragraph that I think is one of the great sentences in the language. It starts 'As they narrated to each other their unholy adventures' and runs through nine 'as' clauses — the laughter forking up like flames, the harpooneers gesticulating with pronged forks, the wind, the sea, the ship groaning — until everything is gathered into one predicate: 'the rushing Pequod, freighted with savages, and laden with fire, and burning a corpse, and plunging into that blackness of darkness, seemed the material counterpart of her monomaniac commander's soul.' Read it aloud once. The syntax is the fire-ship; it piles fuel until the whole vessel and Ahab's mind are a single object. Melville has been telling you for four hundred pages that the ship is Ahab. This is the sentence where he shows it.

Then the thing that actually happens, which is small and terrifying. Ishmael, at the helm for hours, staring at the fiend-shapes, falls into a standing sleep, and wakes 'horribly conscious of something fatally wrong': no compass, a jet gloom, the feeling that the ship is 'not so much bound to any haven ahead as rushing from all havens astern.' He has turned around. He is facing the stern with his back to the compass, and the ship is seconds from flying up into the wind and capsizing. It is the plainest allegory in the book and Melville says so in the next line: 'Look not too long in the face of the fire, O man!' Stare into Ahab's fire and it inverts you — you steer backward with total conviction. This is the moment where Ishmael, who swore the oath on the [[ch36:Death to Moby Dick|quarter-deck]] and forgot it in the [[ch94:I forgot all about our horrible oath|spermaceti]], nearly kills the ship by being an ordinary member of Ahab's crew. It is also, I think, a quiet gloss on [[ch35:Descartian vortices|The Mast-Head]], where the dreamer aloft loses himself in the opposite direction, upward into pantheism; the helm and the mast-head are the two ways a mind goes over the side.

But the chapter isn't done, and the last movement is what I love most. Having preached 'the glorious, golden, glad sun, the only true lamp — all others but liars!' with full conviction, Ishmael immediately takes it back. 'Nevertheless the sun hides not Virginia's Dismal Swamp,' nor the ocean, 'which is the dark side of this earth, and which is two thirds of this earth.' The man 'who hath more of joy than sorrow in him' 'cannot be true — not true, or undeveloped.' 'All is vanity. ALL.' This is the sentence I'd give anyone who thinks the book's darkness is a mood; it is an argument, with proportions — two thirds dark water. And then the resolution, which is not a resolution but a geometry: 'There is a wisdom that is woe; but there is a woe that is madness.' Ishmael lives on the first side of that semicolon; Ahab has crossed to the second; Pip was [[ch93:drowned the infinite of his soul|thrown across]]. The Catskill eagle is Melville's attempt to say how you dive into the blackest gorge and still come out — and his honest admission that some souls fly forever within it, consoled only by the thought that 'that gorge is in the mountains.' The whole moral map of the book, arrived at by way of a near-capsize.

annotations.quote: It is as if from the open field a brick-kiln were transported to her planks.
annotations.note: The chapter opens on an anomaly — masonry aboard a wooden ship — and Melville lets the strangeness sit. Everything that follows grows from this: a furnace where a furnace shouldn't be.

annotations.quote: It was in the left hand try-pot of the Pequod, with the soapstone diligently circling round me, that I was first indirectly struck by the remarkable fact, that in geometry all bodies gliding along the cycloid, my soapstone for example, will descend from any point in precisely the same time.
annotations.note: Ishmael discovers the tautochrone property of the cycloid — a real theorem, Huygens, 1659 — while scrubbing a whale pot. This is the book's method in miniature: the highest abstraction found inside the lowliest labor.

annotations.quote: Like a plethoric burning martyr, or a self-consuming misanthrope, once ignited, the whale supplies his own fuel and burns by his own body.
annotations.note: The whale's scraps feed the fire that renders the whale. Melville can't resist making it a moral image — the martyr, the misanthrope — and it's hard not to hear Ahab in 'self-consuming.'

annotations.quote: It smells like the left wing of the day of judgment; it is an argument for the pit.
annotations.note: Two jokes on top of each other: Judgment Day has a *left wing* (the damned side of a Last Judgment painting), and the stench argues for hell's existence better than any theologian. Melville's humor and his terror are the same instrument.

annotations.quote: then the rushing Pequod, freighted with savages, and laden with fire, and burning a corpse, and plunging into that blackness of darkness, seemed the material counterpart of her monomaniac commander’s soul.
annotations.note: The end of a sentence that began nine clauses earlier with 'As they narrated to each other.' Read the whole paragraph aloud once; the syntax itself is the fire-ship, piling 'as... as... as...' until the ship and Ahab's soul become one object. This is the payoff of a claim the book has made since [[ch41|Moby Dick]] — that the Pequod *is* Ahab — and Melville makes it not by assertion but by grammar: one predicate, holding everything.

annotations.quote: Lo! in my brief sleep I had turned myself about, and was fronting the ship’s stern, with my back to her prow and the compass.
annotations.note: The literal event of the chapter. He fell asleep looking at the fire and woke facing backward with the ship about to capsize — and Melville makes it an allegory so openly that the next paragraph is a sermon.

annotations.quote: Look not too long in the face of the fire, O man! Never dream with thy hand on the helm!
annotations.note: Delivered in the second person, like a proverb, and it is the closest Ishmael comes to warning himself. The 'fire' is Ahab's — the crew has been staring into it since the [[ch36:Death to Moby Dick|quarter-deck]]. Note that the inversion was total and *felt correct*: he grasped the tiller 'convulsively' believing it enchanted. Monomania in this book never feels like error from the inside; it feels like steering.

annotations.quote: the glorious, golden, glad sun, the only true lamp—all others but liars!
annotations.note: Hold this sentence — because the very next paragraph takes it back. Melville states the daylight moral with full conviction and then, being honest, refuses to let it stand.

annotations.quote: The sun hides not the ocean, which is the dark side of this earth, and which is two thirds of this earth. So, therefore, that mortal man who hath more of joy than sorrow in him, that mortal man cannot be true—not true, or undeveloped.
annotations.note: The reversal. Two-thirds of the world is dark water; a sunny man is either false or unfinished. This is the sentence I'd give someone who thinks the book's darkness is a mood — it's an argument, with proportions.

annotations.quote: There is a wisdom that is woe; but there is a woe that is madness.
annotations.note: The whole moral map in twelve words. Ishmael lives on the first side of the semicolon; Ahab has crossed to the second; Pip was thrown across in [[ch93:drowned the infinite of his soul|The Castaway]]. The Catskill eagle that follows is Melville's attempt to say how you dive into the gorge and still come out — and read the last clause honestly: some souls fly 'for ever within the gorge,' and the only consolation offered is that the gorge is high. That is not comfort; it is a very exact description of a life.

links.q: I forgot all about our horrible oath
links.why: The same spermaceti, two chapters earlier, was a bath of kindness; here it is fuel. Melville gives you both faces of the whale's body in a row.
The fire Ishmael stares into is lit here; the Try-Works is what it does to a helmsman.
The other way a mind goes over the side — upward and dreamy at the mast-head, rather than backward at the helm.

links.q: drowned the infinite of his soul
links.why: 'A woe that is madness' has a name aboard: Pip. Read his paragraph beside this one.
Ahab's own sermon on fire, addressed to the corposants — the man who never turns his back to the flame.

ch97.essay:
A page-long chapter that I think of as the book's pilot light. After the hell-fire of the try-works, here is the same oil doing its gentle work: lamps in every bunk, the forecastle a 'shrine of canonized kings,' each sleeping sailor 'a chiselled muteness.' The whaleman, 'as he seeks the food of light, so he lives in light.' It's a small, almost tender restatement of what the whole enterprise is for, and it comes right when you need it.

What strikes me on rereading is the phrase 'the purest of oil, in its unmanufactured, and, therefore, unvitiated state.' Melville has just spent a chapter on the manufacture; now he insists the product at its source is sweeter than anything ashore — 'sweet as early grass butter in April.' The whaleman eats what he kills, and burns it too. There's a whole economics in that: the men who supply the world's light live inside more of it than the customers do.

I don't know whether the effigy imagery — kings and counsellors in oaken vaults — is comforting or funereal. Job 3:14 is behind it: 'with kings and counsellors of the earth, which built desolate places for themselves.' They're asleep, and they look like the dead. The lamps flicker over both readings.

annotations.quote: There they lay in their triangular oaken vaults, each mariner a chiselled muteness; a score of lamps flashing upon his hooded eyes.
annotations.note: Sleeping sailors as tomb effigies. The phrase 'kings and counsellors' just before is from Job — the dead who built desolate places for themselves — so this shrine of light is also a crypt. Melville rarely lets a comfort arrive without its shadow.

annotations.quote: But the whaleman, as he seeks the food of light, so he lives in light.
annotations.note: The chapter's thesis, and a lovely one: the men who supply the world's lamps burn more of the oil than anyone. It's the only trade in the book where the worker gets the product.

annotations.quote: He burns, too, the purest of oil, in its unmanufactured, and, therefore, unvitiated state
annotations.note: Right after a chapter about manufacture, 'unmanufactured' is the key word. Melville's standing preference — raw over refined, the source over the shop — shows up here as a matter of lamp oil.

links.why: Why the whaleman lives in light: because he has just spent a night in fire.
The oil in the lamp is the reason anyone is out here at all; Loomings said so with a shrug.

ch98.essay:
The chapter's real subject is the cycle. Ishmael walks you through the cleanup — hot oil into casks, hammers on hoops, the hold opened 'like a closet walled up,' lye from the whale's own ashes scouring the whale's own grease off the deck — until the ship is 'a spotless dairy room' and the men are strolling 'as bridegrooms new-leaped from out the daintiest Holland,' talking about sofas and carpets. And then: 'There she blows!' and the whole weary thing again.

Melville draws the moral himself, and it's one of the plainest statements of his cosmology: we extract 'from this world's vast bulk its small but valuable sperm,' clean ourselves, learn to live 'in clean tabernacles of the soul,' and then the ghost is spouted up and we sail to fight some other world. I read this as both consoling and exhausting on purpose. 'Oh! my friends, but this is man-killing! Yet this is life.' He won't choose.

The last paragraph is the strangest thing in the chapter, and I keep coming back to it: a sudden apostrophe to Pythagoras — who taught metempsychosis, the transmigration of souls — whom Ishmael claims to have sailed with 'along the Peruvian coast last voyage' as a green simple boy, and taught how to splice a rope. It's a joke about reincarnation and it isn't. If souls come round again like whales and cleanups, then the wisest man in Greece may be a cabin boy, and you may have taught him something. I find that oddly moving.

annotations.quote: like Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, his spermaceti, oil, and bone pass unscathed through the fire
annotations.note: The three men in Nebuchadnezzar's furnace, applied to whale products. It's a joke, and it's also Melville's habit of treating the rendering process as a religious ordeal the whale survives in its essence.

annotations.quote: where once again leviathan returns to his native profundities, sliding along beneath the surface as before; but, alas! never more to rise and blow.
annotations.note: The oil goes into the hold below the waterline, so the whale is 'back' in the deep — in casks. Melville makes the stowing an entombment and a return at once, and lets 'alas!' carry real grief for a creature the book has spent forty chapters butchering.

annotations.quote: from the ashes of the burned scraps of the whale, a potent lye is readily made; and whenever any adhesiveness from the back of the whale remains clinging to the side, that lye quickly exterminates it
annotations.note: The whale cleans up the whale. This closed loop — the animal fuels its own rendering and then scours its own residue — is the kind of fact Melville collects because it looks like a parable without needing to be turned into one.

annotations.quote: fresh and all aglow, as bridegrooms new-leaped from out the daintiest Holland
annotations.note: Holland linen — the men emerge from the filthiest work in the book looking like they've stepped out of a wedding bed. The domestic fantasy that follows (sofas, carpets, tea on the piazza) is comic, and also a real longing on a four-year voyage.

annotations.quote: Oh! my friends, but this is man-killing! Yet this is life.
annotations.note: Two short sentences that refuse to agree with each other. Melville places them side by side and moves on; that refusal to resolve is, I think, the book's honesty about labor.

annotations.quote: hardly is this done, when—_There she blows!_—the ghost is spouted up, and away we sail to fight some other world, and go through young life’s old routine again.
annotations.note: The whale's spout becomes 'the ghost' — a spirit rising — and the cleanup becomes every cleanup in a life: you get the house in order and then the next world arrives. 'Young life's old routine' is a beautiful oxymoron.

annotations.quote: I sailed with thee along the Peruvian coast last voyage—and, foolish as I am, taught thee, a green simple boy, how to splice a rope!
annotations.note: Pythagoras believed souls migrate between bodies, so Ishmael claims to have met him reincarnated as a cabin boy and taught him a knot. It's a gag, but it's also the chapter's cyclical logic taken all the way: nothing is finished, everything comes round, and the wise may be the ones you're teaching.

links.why: The start of the process this chapter closes: cutting-in to stowing-down, one whale's whole passage through the ship.
The fire the deck is being scrubbed clean of.

links.q: There is no steady unretracing progress
links.why: 'There she blows!' again the moment the deck is clean — the cycle Ishmael will make a philosophy of in The Gilder.

ch99.essay:
This is the book's reading lesson, and I think it is the smartest chapter in it. Eight people look at the same coin and the coin says something different to each — and Melville, who has spent four hundred pages making you try to read a whale, now shows you people *reading*, one after another, so you can watch interpretation happen as a spectator sport. The structure is a stage: the mainmast, the coin nailed to it since the [[ch36:whosoever of ye raises me|quarter-deck]], and a series of entrances, with Stubb hiding behind the try-works as chorus.

Ahab goes first, and finds Ahab. 'The firm tower, that is Ahab; the volcano, that is Ahab; the courageous, the undaunted, and victorious fowl, that, too, is Ahab; all are Ahab.' He even supplies the theory: the round gold is 'the image of the rounder globe, which, like a magician's glass, to each and every man in turn but mirrors back his own mysterious self.' Stop on that. Ahab has just explained, correctly, that what you see in the world is your own reflection — and he does not notice that this indicts the whole hunt, that the whale he is chasing across the Pacific may be a mirror. 'Great pains, small gains for those who ask the world to solve them; it cannot solve itself.' He knows. The knowledge changes nothing, and that is the tragic structure of the man in one line. Starbuck finds the Trinity and a 'sun of Righteousness,' then admits the sun 'is no fixture' and walks away 'lest Truth shake me falsely' — his character in miniature, seeing and declining to look longer, exactly as he will at [[ch123|Ahab's cabin door with the musket]]. Stubb gets out the almanac and, in one of the funniest passages in the book, reads the zodiac as the life of man — begotten by the Ram, bumped by the Bull, stung in the rear by the Scorpion, drowned by Aquarius, asleep among the Fishes — and his moral is survival: the sun goes through all of it and 'comes out of it all alive and hearty,' and so does jolly Stubb. Flask finds sixteen dollars, nine hundred and sixty cigars at two cents each. The Manxman finds an omen. Queequeg compares it to his own thigh. Fedallah bows to the sun. Notice that Stubb's aside about the almanac — 'you books must know your places. You'll do to give us the bare words and facts, but we come in to supply the thoughts' — is a complete theory of reading, and it is precisely what the chapter is demonstrating.

Then Pip, and this is the hinge. 'I look, you look, he looks; we look, ye look, they look.' Three times. It is a drill from Murray's Grammar, and it is the only reading in the chapter that is *about reading*. Everyone else conjugates the coin; Pip conjugates the lookers. He alone has been 'watching all of these interpreters — myself included,' as Stubb says, and he alone steps outside the game. The mad boy is the only critic aboard. And his second speech is not nonsense either: 'Here's the ship's navel, this doubloon here, and they are all on fire to unscrew it. But, unscrew your navel, and what's the consequence?' The old joke — unscrew your navel and your bottom falls off — applied to the ship. Pip says the coin is what holds the Pequod together, and everyone wants to take it. He is right in the way prophets in this book are right, which is to say too late.

What unsettles me most is the sentence at the top, before anyone reads: 'some certain significance lurks in all things, else all things are little worth, and the round world itself but an empty cipher.' That is Ishmael's wager, and it is the same wager that terrified him in [[ch42:dumb blankness, full of meaning|The Whiteness of the Whale]] — that the world might be a blank rather than a text. Then he shows you eight incompatible meanings. Is that proof the coin is rich, or proof that meaning is only what the looker brings? I honestly change my mind each time. If Ahab's magician's-glass theory is right, then the whale is a glass too, and the hunt is a man chasing his reflection across an ocean; if Ishmael's wager is right, the eight readings are eight facets of something real. Melville leaves it exactly there, with Pip cawing like a crow from the top of the pine tree, and the coin still nailed where the sunset left it.

annotations.quote: And some certain significance lurks in all things, else all things are little worth, and the round world itself but an empty cipher, except to sell by the cartload, as they do hills about Boston, to fill up some morass in the Milky Way.
annotations.note: Ishmael's wager: meaning must be there or nothing is — the same dread that runs under [[ch42:dumb blankness, full of meaning|The Whiteness of the Whale]], where the blankness might be 'full of meaning' or full of nothing. Then he spends the chapter showing eight people find eight meanings. Decide for yourself whether that confirms the wager or ruins it; I honestly change my mind each time, and I've come to think the chapter is built so that you will too.

annotations.quote: every sunrise found the doubloon where the sunset left it last
annotations.note: A gold coin nailed in the open for years among men Ishmael calls 'ruthless,' and no one touches it. It's sanctified. The crew's superstition is stronger than their greed, which tells you what kind of ship this is.

annotations.quote: The firm tower, that is Ahab; the volcano, that is Ahab; the courageous, the undaunted, and victorious fowl, that, too, is Ahab; all are Ahab
annotations.note: Ahab reads the coin and finds only himself, three times. He even says why — the world is 'a magician's glass' that mirrors the looker — and doesn't notice that this indicts his whole hunt: if the coin is a mirror, so is the whale. Compare [[ch36:pasteboard masks|the pasteboard-mask speech]], where he insists there is something *behind* the mask. Here he says there's only a glass. He holds both beliefs and acts on the first.

annotations.quote: Great pains, small gains for those who ask the world to solve them; it cannot solve itself.
annotations.note: Ahab, of all people, says this. He knows the world can't answer, and he'll demand an answer anyway. This is the tragic structure in one line: the knowledge doesn't change the action.

annotations.quote: This coin speaks wisely, mildly, truly, but still sadly to me. I will quit it, lest Truth shake me falsely.
annotations.note: Starbuck finds Christian hope on the coin and then admits the sun 'is no fixture' — there's no solace at midnight. He walks away before the reading can finish. That retreat is his character in miniature: he sees, and declines to look longer.

annotations.quote: Book! you lie there; the fact is, you books must know your places. You’ll do to give us the bare words and facts, but we come in to supply the thoughts.
annotations.note: Stubb, almanac in hand, states a whole theory of reading: texts supply facts, readers supply meaning. It's a joke and it's also exactly what this chapter is demonstrating.

annotations.quote: There’s a sermon now, writ in high heaven, and the sun goes through it every year, and yet comes out of it all alive and hearty.
annotations.note: Stubb's zodiac — begotten, bumped, stung, drowned, asleep — is the funniest life story in the book, and his moral is survival: the sun goes through it all and comes out jolly. It's the cheerful man's cosmology, and Melville gives it real charm.

annotations.quote: It is worth sixteen dollars, that’s true; and at two cents the cigar, that’s nine hundred and sixty cigars.
annotations.note: Flask's reading. After the Trinity and the zodiac, someone does the arithmetic. Melville lets it be stupid and also lets it be the only reading that's simply *correct* — the coin is, in fact, money.

annotations.quote: “I look, you look, he looks; we look, ye look, they look.”
annotations.note: Pip's grammar drill is the hinge of the chapter. Everyone else reads the coin; Pip reads the readers, conjugating the act of looking itself — and Stubb's aside tells you Pip 'has been watching all of these interpreters, myself included.' The one they call mad is the only one standing outside the game, which is the same position Ishmael occupies as narrator. That is why Stubb can't bear him: 'he's too crazy-witty for my sanity.'

annotations.quote: Here’s the ship’s navel, this doubloon here, and they are all on fire to unscrew it. But, unscrew your navel, and what’s the consequence?
annotations.note: The old joke — unscrew your navel and your bottom falls off — applied to the ship. Pip says the doubloon is what holds the Pequod together, and they all want to take it. He's right, in the way prophets in this book are right.

annotations.quote: Stand away again and hear him. Hark!
annotations.note: Stubb has turned the mainmast into a theatre and himself into the audience — 'dodge round the try-works,' 'stand away again.' Melville is staging interpretation as performance, and the comic device (a mate hiding behind a furnace) lets him line up eight readings without ever telling you which is right.

links.why: Where the coin was nailed up and what it was promised for; the doubloon is the quarter-deck vow made into an object.
The fear underneath this chapter: that a thing might be read eight ways because it says nothing at all.

links.q: He saw God’s foot upon the treadle
links.why: Why Pip, of all the readers, is the one who can see the looking itself.
Starbuck 'quits' the coin 'lest Truth shake me falsely'; here he quits the loaded musket the same way.

links.q: Ahab never thinks; he only feels
links.why: The last reading of the doubloon is Ahab's own, on the third day — and it's not a reading, it's a feeling.

ch100.essay:
Ahab meets a man who has the same wound and drew the opposite conclusion. Captain Boomer lost an arm to Moby Dick, crossed his wake twice since, and 'didn't want to try to: ain't one limb enough?' He's cheerful, bluff, a drinker, and he's got a surgeon who is one of the great comic characters in the book — Dr. Bunger, the teetotaler who won't drink water, with a dent in his skull that he was born with. The whole chapter is a gam that Ahab experiences as an obstruction: two Englishmen ribbing each other while he wants only one fact, *which way heading*.

The entrance is my favorite passage. Ahab, so eager he forgets he can't climb a ship's side, is reduced 'to a clumsy landsman again,' and has to be hoisted aboard in a blubber-hook like a carcass. Then the two men touch ivory to ivory — 'let us shake bones together!' — 'an arm that never can shrink, d'ye see; and a leg that never can run.' Melville stages the meeting of the maimed as both grotesque and tender. Boomer is what Ahab could have been: wounded, and done.

And the counter-theory arrives in Bunger's mouth, as a joke: the whale's malice 'is only his awkwardness.' He can't digest an arm; he never means to swallow one; he only 'thinks to terrify by feints.' Ahab's entire metaphysics — that the whale is intentional evil — is dismissed in one drunken surgeon's aside, and Ahab doesn't argue, he just leaves. 'He's all a magnet!' What is best let alone is not always what least allures. The chapter ends with Ahab's back to a man who could have saved him, 'face set like a flint to his own' ship. That's Isaiah's phrase for the prophet who will not be turned.

annotations.quote: and one empty arm of this jacket streamed behind him like the broidered arm of a hussar’s surcoat
annotations.note: Before we know he's lost an arm, we see the empty sleeve as military finery. Boomer wears his loss lightly, almost as decoration — and that lightness is the whole contrast with Ahab, who wears his as a weapon.

annotations.quote: Ahab now found himself abjectly reduced to a clumsy landsman again; hopelessly eyeing the uncertain changeful height he could hardly hope to attain
annotations.note: A rare moment of Ahab helpless in front of strangers. He'd forgotten, in his eagerness, that he can't climb a ship. It's a small humiliation, and Melville tells us these small ones are what most inflame him.

annotations.quote: slid his solitary thigh into the curve of the hook (it was like sitting in the fluke of an anchor, or the crotch of an apple tree)
annotations.note: Ahab is hoisted aboard in a blubber-hook — the same tackle that lifts dead whales. The apple-tree parenthesis is almost gentle, which makes the grotesque underneath it worse.

annotations.quote: let us shake bones together!—an arm and a leg!—an arm that never can shrink, d’ye see; and a leg that never can run.
annotations.note: Two prosthetics crossed 'like two sword-fish blades.' Ahab's joke is bitter and exact: ivory limbs are loyal because they're dead. It's the closest thing to fellowship he allows himself in the book, and it lasts about a page.

annotations.quote: “Aye, aye—they were mine—_my_ irons,” cried Ahab, exultingly
annotations.note: Boomer mentions harpoons near the whale's fin and Ahab claims them like a lover recognizing his letters. 'Exultingly' is the word to notice — he is happy, here, for a moment, to know his iron is still in the whale.

annotations.quote: that thing is against all rule”—pointing at it with the marlingspike—“that is the captain’s work, not mine; he ordered the carpenter to make it; he had that club-hammer there put to the end, to knock some one’s brains out with
annotations.note: Boomer's ivory arm ends in a mallet — a comic version of Ahab's leg, which is also a made thing with a purpose. The surgeon disowns it. Note that Ahab will be sitting with his own carpenter in a few chapters, commissioning a new leg.

annotations.quote: Didn’t want to try to: ain’t one limb enough? What should I do without this other arm?
annotations.note: The sane answer to Moby Dick, in one line. Boomer has the same injury, the same whale, twice the opportunity — and simply declines. Melville puts this man in front of Ahab and lets Ahab walk past him.

annotations.quote: So that what you take for the White Whale’s malice is only his awkwardness. For he never means to swallow a single limb; he only thinks to terrify by feints.
annotations.note: Bunger, half-joking, dismantles Ahab's theology: the whale isn't evil, it's clumsy. Nobody in the book states the naturalist's case more plainly, and it's delivered by a comic drunk who's about to try to bleed Ahab with a lancet.

annotations.quote: What is best let alone, that accursed thing is not always what least allures. He’s all a magnet!
annotations.note: Ahab agrees the whale is best let alone, and says that's exactly why he can't. He knows. The tragedy isn't ignorance; it's that knowledge has no purchase on him.

annotations.quote: With back to the stranger ship, and face set like a flint to his own, Ahab stood upright till alongside of the Pequod.
annotations.note: 'I have set my face like a flint' is Isaiah 50:7 — the servant who will not be turned from his suffering. Melville gives Ahab a prophet's posture as he turns away from the one man who could have talked him out of it.

links.why: Ahab's leg, first seen; Boomer's arm is its cheerful double.
What the ivory leg actually costs Ahab, told right after this.
The other ship that met the White Whale and came away with a warning; Gabriel's version of Boomer's shrug.

links.q: it is a mild, mild wind
links.why: The one moment Ahab nearly takes Boomer's advice.

ch101.essay:
After the intensity of Leg and Arm, Melville pours a drink. This chapter is a shaggy-dog tribute to English whaling hospitality that ends up as a statistical table of Dutch provisions — 400,000 pounds of beef, 10,800 barrels of beer — and a calculation that each Low Dutch seaman got two barrels of beer for twelve weeks. It's Ishmael at his most digressive and I've come to think the digressiveness is the point: he's proving that life goes on, that after a man has stared at the whale and turned away there is still flip and dumplings and a squall you're too drunk to reef for.

The drunken-furling scene — jackets reefed into the sails, men hanging in the gale 'a warning example to all drunken tars' — is one of those anecdotes Ishmael drops that has nothing to do with the Pequod's voyage. He boarded the Samuel Enderby 'long, very long after old Ahab touched her planks.' So Ishmael survived, and went to sea again, and had a good time. That's an odd thing to be told in the middle of a tragedy, and it changes how you hear the rest.

The fake scholarship — Dr. Snodhead, professor at 'the college of Santa Claus and St. Pott's,' translating 'Dan Coopman' by Fitz Swackhammer — is Melville teasing his own encyclopedic method. He knows the cetology is half a put-on. He wants you to know he knows.

annotations.quote: A short life to them, and a jolly death.
annotations.note: A sailor's toast, inverted from 'long life.' Ishmael means it warmly, and it's chilling in a book that is about to deliver a short life and a decidedly unjolly death to nearly everyone aboard.

annotations.quote: And that fine gam I had—long, very long after old Ahab touched her planks with his ivory heel
annotations.note: Quietly, the chapter tells you Ishmael lives long past the Pequod and sails again. It's one of a handful of places the book leaks its own ending — and the leak arrives disguised as a drinking story.

annotations.quote: we ignorantly furled the skirts of our jackets into the sails, so that we hung there, reefed fast in the howling gale, a warning example to all drunken tars
annotations.note: Men sewn into the sails by their own drunkenness, dangling in a gale. It's a genuinely funny image and also a small vision of what the sea does to the careless: it takes you up with the canvas.

annotations.quote: my friend Dr. Snodhead, a very learned man, professor of Low Dutch and High German in the college of Santa Claus and St. Pott’s
annotations.note: Melville invents a scholar, a college, an author (Fitz Swackhammer), and a book, and then cites them with a straight face. It's a wink at every footnote in the cetological chapters: how much of this did you believe?

annotations.quote: Most statistical tables are parchingly dry in the reading; not so in the present case, however, where the reader is flooded with whole pipes, barrels, quarts, and gills of good gin and good cheer.
annotations.note: A pun that's also a thesis about Melville's method — that a list can be a pleasure, and that quantity itself can be a kind of poetry. He believes it; the Extracts at the front of the book are the same idea.

annotations.quote: For, say they, when cruising in an empty ship, if you can get nothing better out of the world, get a good dinner out of it, at least.
annotations.note: The chapter's quiet moral, and a sane one. Set it against Ahab, who has an empty ship and will not eat. The English captain's philosophy is here in a proverb: if the world won't give you the whale, take the dinner.

links.why: The Samuel Enderby's hospitality is the occasion for this whole excursion into beef and beer.
The Advocate — the earlier, more strenuous defense of whaling's honor that this chapter turns into a feast.

ch102.essay:
I think this is the secret center of the cetological chapters, and it is disguised as a travelogue with a comic frame. Ishmael, challenged by himself by name — 'But how now, Ishmael? How is it, that you, a mere oarsman in the fishery, pretend to know aught about the subterranean parts of the whale?' — answers with a story about his 'late royal friend Tranquo, king of Tranque,' and a whale skeleton kept in a temple of palms in a jungle glen. The answer is glorious nonsense offered with total confidence, and it is also the occasion for the book's most serious theological paragraph. Melville often hides his deepest things inside his silliest frames; here he hides a cosmology inside an alibi.

The paragraph is the one that begins 'It was a wondrous sight.' The forest is a loom — 'the industrious earth beneath was as a weaver's loom,' the vines the warp and woof, the flowers the figures, the sun 'a flying shuttle weaving the unwearied verdure.' Then Ishmael does something no one else in the book does: he addresses the weaver directly. 'Oh, busy weaver! unseen weaver! — pause! — one word! — whither flows the fabric? what palace may it deck? wherefore all these ceaseless toilings? Speak, weaver! — stay thy hand!' It is Ahab's question — why won't the universe explain itself? — asked in Ishmael's voice, without rage. And the answer is not silence and not malice. 'The weaver-god, he weaves; and by that weaving is he deafened, that he hears no mortal voice.' God cannot hear you, not because he will not but because his own work is too loud. The universe is not indifferent; it is a *factory*, and 'we, too, who look on the loom are deafened.' This is Pip's vision from [[ch93:He saw God’s foot upon the treadle|The Castaway]] — God's foot on the treadle — expanded from a glimpse into a mechanism, and it grows out of the mat Ishmael and Queequeg wove in [[ch47:chance, free will, and necessity|The Mat-Maker]], where the loom was a metaphor for how a life gets made. Here the metaphor has become the world.

Then comes the turn I find most mysterious, and I want to be honest that I don't fully understand it. The words inaudible among the flying spindles 'are plainly heard without the walls, bursting from the opened casements. Thereby have villainies been detected. Ah, mortal! then, be heedful; for so, in all this din of the great world's loom, thy subtlest thinkings may be overheard afar.' Is it a warning — someone outside the world can hear what you think inside it? Or a consolation — nothing said in the noise is finally lost? I have read it as both, and I now suspect Melville left it undecided on purpose, because the book keeps returning to the question of who is listening: Ahab defying the fire in [[ch119:right worship is defiance|The Candles]], Pip praying to the 'big white God aloft' in [[ch40:Oh, thou big white God aloft there|Midnight, Forecastle]]. The Arsacides says: perhaps someone hears — but only from outside the mill.

And the skeleton itself. 'Life folded Death; Death trellised Life; the grim god wived with youthful Life, and begat him curly-headed glories' — vines on bones stated as a marriage, and the sentence stops describing and starts chanting. Then Ishmael goes inside with a ball of twine, Theseus in the labyrinth, and comes out: 'I saw no living thing within; naught was there but bones.' Nine words after a page of ecstatic weaving. He went into the god and found it empty, and still the vines grow. That contrast is the book's whole nervous system, and it is why I can't take the deafened weaver as simple despair: the emptiness at the center doesn't stop the weaving at the edges.

The comedy at the end matters too. The priests keep 'an unextinguished aromatic flame' in the skull so the dead god appears to spout, and swear the smoke is genuine — Melville's quiet description of every religion he knew. They object not to measurement but to *who* measures, then brawl over feet and inches with their yardsticks. Sir Clifford in Yorkshire charges twopence for the whispering gallery in the spine. And Ishmael has the dimensions tattooed on his right arm, keeping the rest of his body 'a blank page for a poem.' Statistics on the arm, verse on the body: the two halves of this book, and of Queequeg, whose tattoos are [[ch110:but whose mysteries not even himself could read|a treatise he cannot read]] and will be copied onto the coffin that saves the narrator. Everything in this jungle is connected to everything in the ship; that's what a loom is.

annotations.quote: But how now, Ishmael? How is it, that you, a mere oarsman in the fishery, pretend to know aught about the subterranean parts of the whale?
annotations.note: Ishmael interrogates himself by name. It's a real question — where does a foremast hand get anatomical authority? — and the answer that follows (a king in the Arsacides, a tattooed forearm) is glorious nonsense offered with total confidence.

annotations.quote: in the skull, the priests kept up an unextinguished aromatic flame, so that the mystic head again sent forth its vapory spout
annotations.note: The priests fake the whale's spout with incense. Melville is quietly describing every religion he knows: keep a fire in the skull of the dead thing so it appears to breathe. Ishmael marvels that they 'swear that smoky jet of his was genuine.'

annotations.quote: Oh, busy weaver! unseen weaver!—pause!—one word!—whither flows the fabric? what palace may it deck? wherefore all these ceaseless toilings? Speak, weaver!—stay thy hand!—but one single word with thee!
annotations.note: Ishmael asks God the only question that matters — what is it for? — and gets no answer because the loom is too loud. This is, for me, the book's central theological image, and it isn't cruelty or absence: it's deafening industry.

annotations.quote: The weaver-god, he weaves; and by that weaving is he deafened, that he hears no mortal voice
annotations.note: God can't hear you, not because he won't but because his own work drowns you out. Compare Pip in [[ch93:He saw God’s foot upon the treadle|The Castaway]] — 'God's foot upon the treadle' — which was a glimpse; this is the full mechanism. What I find remarkable is that Melville chose *noise* over absence or malice. Ahab believes in a malicious agent behind the mask; the Arsacides proposes something more modern and, to me, more frightening: an agent too busy making the world to attend to anything in it.

annotations.quote: Ah, mortal! then, be heedful; for so, in all this din of the great world’s loom, thy subtlest thinkings may be overheard afar.
annotations.note: The turn I find most mysterious. What's inaudible inside the mill is heard clearly outside it — so your quietest thoughts might be audible somewhere beyond the world. A warning, or a consolation? 'Thereby have villainies been detected' tilts it toward warning; 'be heedful' confirms it; and yet the image of voices 'bursting from the opened casements' is almost hopeful. I genuinely don't know, and I think Melville didn't decide. Hold it beside Ahab's defiance in [[ch119:right worship is defiance|The Candles]] — a man shouting into the loom, betting someone hears.

annotations.quote: Life folded Death; Death trellised Life; the grim god wived with youthful Life, and begat him curly-headed glories.
annotations.note: Vines on a skeleton, stated as a marriage. Melville's sentences often reach a point where they stop describing and start chanting; this is one, and the 'curly-headed glories' are both flowers and children.

annotations.quote: I saw no living thing within; naught was there but bones.
annotations.note: He goes inside the god with a ball of twine, Theseus in the labyrinth, and finds nothing living. Nine words, and they land after a page of ecstatic weaving. That contrast is the book's whole nervous system.

annotations.quote: “Dar’st thou measure this our god! That’s for us.”
annotations.note: The priests object not to measurement but to *who* measures. Then they fall to brawling over feet and inches. Melville's view of religious authority is compressed here: the mystery is guarded by men arguing about yardsticks.

annotations.quote: Sir Clifford thinks of charging twopence for a peep at the whispering gallery in the spinal column; threepence to hear the echo in the hollow of his cerebellum; and sixpence for the unrivalled view from his forehead.
annotations.note: The English lord's whale is a paid attraction with trap-doors and a footman with keys. Melville places it beside the Arsacidean temple and doesn't say which is the more absurd form of worship.

annotations.quote: wished the other parts of my body to remain a blank page for a poem I was then composing
annotations.note: The skeleton's dimensions are tattooed on Ishmael's right arm, the rest of him reserved for poetry. Statistics on the arm, verse on the body — the two halves of this book, and of Queequeg, whose tattoos are [[ch110:but whose mysteries not even himself could read|a whole cosmology he can't read]]. The joke about being 'crowded for space' is also a confession: the book itself is crowded, and Melville chose to leave the odd inches out.

annotations.quote: the mighty idler seemed the cunning weaver; himself all woven over with the vines
annotations.note: The bones, which do nothing, look like the weaver of the vines that cover them. That optical trick — the dead thing at the center seeming to author the life at the edges — is as close as Melville comes to saying what he thinks a god is.

links.why: The loom began as a mat on a quiet afternoon; here it has become the world. Read them in order.

links.q: He saw God’s foot upon the treadle
links.why: Pip saw the weaver's foot and went mad; Ishmael hears the whole machine and writes a chapter.

links.q: but whose mysteries not even himself could read
links.why: Queequeg's tattoos, Ishmael's tattooed arm, and the coffin: the body as unreadable text.
Ahab's answer to the deafened weaver — shout louder.
The measurements themselves, straight off the arm; skip it if you like, but it's the punchline of the tattoo.

ch103.essay:
The plainest chapter in this stretch, and I like it for its plainness — and for the way it keeps undercutting itself. Ishmael delivers the numbers he promised: seventy-two feet of skeleton, ten ribs a side, forty-odd vertebrae, ninety tons of living whale, 'thirteen men to a ton.' The comparison to a village of eleven hundred people is exactly the kind of scale trick that makes you feel the size instead of just reading it.

But the chapter's real argument is against itself. The whale's skeleton 'is by no means the mould of his invested form': the biggest rib is eight feet where the living body was sixteen deep; the fins are a few disordered joints; the flukes, 'weighty and majestic, but boneless,' are 'an utter blank!' So the skeleton is a bad map. 'How vain and foolish, then... to try to comprehend aright this wondrous whale, by merely poring over his dead attenuated skeleton.' Only in peril, only in the sea, can the whale be 'truly and livingly found out.' Ishmael measures, and then says measuring won't do. That double motion — collect the facts, deny their sufficiency — is how the whole cetology works.

And the ending is perfect: the smallest tail-bones are gone because the priests' children stole them for marbles. 'Thus we see how that the spine of even the hugest of living things tapers off at last into simple child's play.' It's a joke, and it's also where Melville's mind always goes — the immense dwindles into the domestic, the cosmic god has kids playing with its bones.

annotations.quote: reckoning thirteen men to a ton, he would considerably outweigh the combined population of a whole village of one thousand one hundred inhabitants
annotations.note: Ninety tons means nothing; a village does. Melville is always looking for the unit that makes a number felt, and here it's people — the whale weighs a town.

annotations.quote: you must not fail to carry it in your mind, or under your arm, as we proceed
annotations.note: Carry the twenty-foot skull under your arm. Ishmael treats the reader as a museum visitor being handed exhibits, and the absurdity is the charm — you're meant to feel how impossible the assembly is.

annotations.quote: the skeleton of the whale is by no means the mould of his invested form
annotations.note: The chapter's warning about its own method. The bones don't tell you the shape of the living thing — and the book has spent hundreds of pages assembling bones. Melville knows the limit of his own encyclopedia and states it here.

annotations.quote: and in place of the weighty and majestic, but boneless flukes, an utter blank!
annotations.note: The most powerful part of the whale — the tail Ishmael devoted a whole chapter to — leaves nothing in the skeleton. What matters most is what doesn't survive. That's a hard thought for a book about remembering the dead.

annotations.quote: Only in the heart of quickest perils; only when within the eddyings of his angry flukes; only on the profound unbounded sea, can the fully invested whale be truly and livingly found out.
annotations.note: Knowledge requires danger. This is Ishmael's epistemology in one sentence, and it's also, uncomfortably, Ahab's — the difference being that Ishmael wants to *know* the whale and Ahab wants to kill it.

annotations.quote: Thus we see how that the spine of even the hugest of living things tapers off at last into simple child’s play.
annotations.note: The priests' children stole the smallest vertebrae for marbles. Melville can't resist: the god's spine ends in a game. It's a small sentence that carries the book's whole sense of scale — the immense always dwindles into somebody's pocket.

links.why: Where these numbers were tattooed, and why the odd inches are missing.
The Tail: the other place Ishmael measures and admits the measurement misses the thing.

links.q: God keep me from ever completing anything
links.why: Cetology's confession that the system will never be finished; this is a chapter of a book that knows it.

ch104.essay:
