This is the chapter where Melville tells you what he's doing. 'To produce a mighty book, you must choose a mighty theme. No great and enduring volume can ever be written on the flea, though many there be who have tried it.' He's a third of the way from the end of a book that has been accused, ever since, of bigness for its own sake, and here he says: yes, on purpose. 'Give me a condor's quill! Give me Vesuvius' crater for an inkstand!' The joke about needing Johnson's dictionary because Johnson himself was fat enough to compile a whale author's lexicon is pure Melville — the grandiloquence and the self-mockery in one breath.

The fossil material is real: Cuvier, Owen, the Basilosaurus that turned out to be a whale (Zeuglodon), the Alabama plantation where enslaved people took the bones for a fallen angel. Melville folds it into geology's deep time, which in 1851 was still a new and frightening idea — and then goes further than geology: 'time began with man,' so the whale is before time, 'antemosaic, unsourced.' 'Ahab's harpoon had shed older blood than the Pharaoh's.' That sentence is the chapter for me: the hunt is not a man against an animal but a man against something older than history, and the horror Ishmael feels is precise — an existence that was before all time 'must needs exist after all humane ages are over.' The whale will outlast us. Ahab is picking a fight with that.

It ends in John Leo's African temple of whale bones, where Ishmael leaves you to 'silently worship.' Three temples in three chapters — Arsacidean, English, Barbary. Everyone builds a church out of the whale.

annotations.quote: Give me a condor’s quill! Give me Vesuvius’ crater for an inkstand! Friends, hold my arms!
annotations.note: Melville performing his own inflation, and knowing it. 'Friends, hold my arms!' is the line of a man about to write something enormous and asking to be restrained — the book's self-awareness at its most delighted.

annotations.quote: To produce a mighty book, you must choose a mighty theme. No great and enduring volume can ever be written on the flea, though many there be who have tried it.
annotations.note: The most-quoted sentence in the chapter, and it's a genuine artistic credo: scale is a choice. Melville had written five sea-yarns before this and knew the difference. The flea joke keeps it from being pompous.

annotations.quote: because that famous lexicographer’s uncommon personal bulk more fitted him to compile a lexicon to be used by a whale author like me
annotations.note: He uses Johnson's dictionary because Johnson was fat. This is the sort of joke that tells you Melville is enjoying himself — and 'whale author' is, I think, the job title he'd have put on a card.

annotations.quote: The awe-stricken credulous slaves in the vicinity took it for the bones of one of the fallen angels.
annotations.note: Three readings of one skeleton: the enslaved see an angel, the Alabama doctors see a reptile, Owen in London sees a whale. It's the Doubloon again, in bone — and the 'credulous' reading is not obviously the least true.

annotations.quote: I am, by a flood, borne back to that wondrous period, ere time itself can be said to have begun; for time began with man.
annotations.note: A startling claim: no man, no time. The whale, then, lived before time. Melville takes the new geology and pushes it past science into vertigo.

annotations.quote: Ahab’s harpoon had shed older blood than the Pharaoh’s. Methuselah seems a school-boy.
annotations.note: The hunt reframed: Ahab isn't fighting an animal but an antiquity. Every harpoon in the book is now striking something older than Egypt, and the second sentence makes the oldest man in the Bible a child beside it.

annotations.quote: I am horror-struck at this antemosaic, unsourced existence of the unspeakable terrors of the whale, which, having been before all time, must needs exist after all humane ages are over.
annotations.note: The whale will outlast humanity. Ishmael calls this horror, and I think it's the real source of the book's dread — not that the whale is evil, but that it's permanent and we aren't.

annotations.quote: In this Afric Temple of the Whale I leave you, reader, and if you be a Nantucketer, and a whaleman, you will silently worship there.
annotations.note: Third temple of bones in three chapters. Melville ends by inviting worship, and I don't think it's ironic: he's spent a hundred chapters making the whale a god, and here he opens the door.

links.why: The forward-looking half of this pair: from pre-Adamite seas to the last flood.
The other place Ishmael demands a bigger pen for a bigger subject.
The Sub-Sub-Librarian's heap of whale-lore; the Fossil Whale is that method applied to geology.

ch105.essay:
Ishmael asks two questions — has the whale shrunk since ancient times, and will he be hunted out of existence — and answers no to both with complete confidence, and history has proved him wrong on the second. Reading this chapter in the twenty-first century is a peculiar experience, and I want to explain why I love it anyway rather than just note that it aged badly.

The first argument is the good one. Pliny's whales covering acres, Aldrovandus's eight hundred feet — 'Rope Walks and Thames Tunnels of Whales!' — and Ishmael's flat refusal: 'will any whaleman believe these stories? No.' His authority is the tape-measure, and it entitles him, he thinks, to argue with the dead: 'if ever I go where Pliny is, I, a whaleman (more than he was), will make bold to tell him so.' That parenthesis is the whole book's attitude toward learned sources, the same one that made him rank the [[ch55|painters of whales]] by whether they had ever seen one. Then the reasoning about extinction, and here is what I find most remarkable: the counterargument is *right there*, and he sees it perfectly. The buffalo, 'not forty years ago,' overspread the prairies by tens of thousands 'where now the polite broker sells you land at a dollar an inch'; 'not one horn or hoof of them remains in all that region; and though the cause of this wondrous extermination was the spear of man.' He has the whole American pattern — herd, slaughter, subdivision — and he argues past it. Forty men in a ship are thrilled with forty whales in forty-eight months, whereas forty mounted hunters would kill forty thousand buffalo; the whale has 'a pasture to expatiate in' twice the size of all the continents; several adult generations overlap because whales live a century; and the whale-bone whales have their 'two firm fortresses,' the Polar citadels, where 'in a charmed circle of everlasting December' they 'bid defiance to all pursuit from man.'

All of it was reasonable in 1851. None of it survived the explosive harpoon, the steam catcher, and the factory ship, and the 'charmed circle of everlasting December' is exactly where the twentieth century killed most of them. I can't read that phrase without a small ache — Ishmael's safe place was the killing ground. But I think the chapter is more than a period piece, because it is the most honest picture in the book of how intelligent people reason about extinction: with all the evidence in hand, and a conclusion chosen in advance. 'But you must look at this matter in every light' introduces a genuine attempt at fairness, with real numbers, that arrives where the author needed it to. It is a portrait of reasoning under hope, and it reads very differently now than it did then. It also belongs to the book's larger argument about the whale's *unkillability*, which Ahab needs and Ishmael half-believes: the same faith that in [[ch41|Moby Dick]] made the crew whisper that the White Whale was ubiquitous and immortal.

And then the last paragraph, which is glorious regardless of whether it is true. 'We account the whale immortal in his species, however perishable in his individuality.' He swam over the site of the Tuileries and Windsor Castle and the Kremlin before the continents broke water; 'in Noah's flood he despised Noah's Ark'; and when the world is flooded again 'to kill off its rats,' the eternal whale will rear 'upon the topmost crest of the equatorial flood' and 'spout his frothed defiance to the skies.' It is a hymn, and it is the whale Ahab is about to meet — not an animal but the thing that was here before the continents and expects to be here after. That is what makes the sentence about individuality so strange when you carry it into the Chase. Ahab will kill nothing that matters, and be killed by something that, on this chapter's theology, can't die; and yet the creature that actually breaks the Pequod is an individual, scarred, harpoon-stuck, and mortal. Melville lets both be true. The [[ch104:I am, by a flood, borne back to that wondrous period|Fossil Whale]] chapter just before this one looked backward to the pre-Adamite oceans; this one looks forward to the last flood; between them the Pequod is sailing through a very small window of time, and the book knows it. I read the chapter as a monument to a confidence the world took away, and I love it because Ishmael's error is not stupidity — it is the size of his love for the animal.

annotations.quote: Rope Walks and Thames Tunnels of Whales!
annotations.note: Ishmael's response to Aldrovandus's eight-hundred-foot whale: an exclamation of pure scorn dressed as wonder. He is a whaleman, and whalemen believe their tape-measures over the ancients.

annotations.quote: And if ever I go where Pliny is, I, a whaleman (more than he was), will make bold to tell him so.
annotations.note: He'll correct Pliny in the afterlife. Ishmael's authority is experience, and it entitles him, he thinks, to argue with the dead. The parenthesis is the whole book's attitude toward learned sources.

annotations.quote: whether he must not at last be exterminated from the waters, and the last whale, like the last man, smoke his last pipe, and then himself evaporate in the final puff
annotations.note: The extinction question, stated with a strange gentleness — the last whale as the last smoker. Read the rest of the chapter knowing that his answer, 'no,' was wrong within a century.

annotations.quote: where now the polite broker sells you land at a dollar an inch
annotations.note: The buffalo grounds are now real estate. Melville saw the whole American pattern — herd, slaughter, subdivision — clearly, and sets it down as the counterargument he then talks himself out of.

annotations.quote: But you must look at this matter in every light.
annotations.note: Watch what follows this sentence: a genuine attempt to be fair, with real numbers, that arrives at the conclusion the author wanted. It's a portrait of reasoning under hope, and it reads differently now than it did in 1851.

annotations.quote: in a charmed circle of everlasting December, bid defiance to all pursuit from man
annotations.note: The Polar refuge. It's a lovely phrase and it's exactly where the factory ships went in the twentieth century. I can't read it without a small ache — Ishmael's safe place was the killing ground. Notice, too, the martial vocabulary: 'fortresses,' 'citadels,' 'battalions,' 'bid defiance.' He is imagining the whales as a nation at war, which is generous, and wrong about who had the better weapons.

annotations.quote: by imagining all the grave-yards, cemeteries, and family vaults of creation yielding up the live bodies of all the men, women, and children who were alive seventy-five years ago; and adding this countless host to the present human population
annotations.note: To explain overlapping whale generations, he raises the human dead. It's a resurrection image used as demography, and it's the kind of comparison only Melville reaches for — the census as apocalypse.

annotations.quote: we account the whale immortal in his species, however perishable in his individuality
annotations.note: The chapter's conclusion, and it's the book's theology of the whale in a phrase: the individual dies, the kind persists. Ahab will kill nothing that matters and be killed by something that can't die — and yet the whale of the [[ch133|Chase]] is emphatically an individual, with a wrinkled brow and old irons in his side. Melville holds species-immortality and one scarred body together, and never says which is Moby Dick.

annotations.quote: then the eternal whale will still survive, and rearing upon the topmost crest of the equatorial flood, spout his frothed defiance to the skies.
annotations.note: The last image before the narrative resumes: the whale on the crest of the world's final flood, spouting at heaven. That's the creature the Pequod is sailing toward, and you're meant to carry this picture into the Chase.

links.q: I am, by a flood, borne back to that wondrous period
links.why: The chapter before looks back to pre-Adamite seas; this one looks forward to the last flood. Read them as one long span of time.
The crew's superstition that Moby Dick is immortal — and Ishmael's rational version of it, here.
The Grand Armada, where the 'vast but widely separated, unfrequent armies' he mentions are actually seen, nursing their young.

links.q: from hell’s heart I stab at thee
links.why: The individual whale, mortal and scarred, meets the man who cannot kill the species.
